Re-run the calibration on recent traffic on a schedule, alert on the strong-call share and the fallback rate, and keep the shadow sample running.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: RANSAC: keeping only matches that agree on one homography
md: A homography is only correct for planar scenes or pure camera rotation. For a general 3D scene seen from two positions, matches satisfy a fundamental or essential matrix instead, and forcing a homography will reject many correct matches.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: Freeing nodes safely: hazard pointers and epochs
md: EBR is fast because readers only write their own epoch when they pin, but it is not strictly lock-free for memory: Fraser notes that a process that stalls inside a critical region stops the limbo lists (Fraser's name for the per-epoch garbage bags) from ever being reclaimed. Hazard pointers bound the unreclaimed memory (at most NR nodes) at the cost of publishing and re-validating every pointer before use.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: Drift when a release changes the format, and a pipeline that holds
md: The whole course in one line: a log template is the cheapest useful abstraction over log text, and the only one that turns an unbounded stream of unique strings into a small set of countable events. Everything after it, counting, baselining, sequence models, dashboards, inherits both its power and its errors.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Sigma: one rule format, many SIEMs
md: A converted query is only as right as its pipeline's field mapping. If your SIEM stores Sysmon in a different source, or the 4688 field is NewProcessName rather than Image, the query is valid, runs, and silently matches nothing. Always test converted rules against real events from your own environment.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Position Interpolation and NTK-aware scaling
md: Uniform interpolation protects the slow pairs but blurs the fast ones. Every better method since PI is about treating pairs differently according to their wavelength.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Build it: YaRN tables and a four-host ring in NumPy
md: The paper's YaRN and Hugging Face's YaRN are different functions in the middle pairs. A checkpoint fine-tuned under one and served under the other sees frequencies it was not trained with. When porting a model between frameworks, compare the generated inv_freq tables, not just the config keys.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: What a loop can compute: algorithms, latent thoughts, fixed points
md: Convergence is not automatic. The toy update halves the distance to its fixed point each step (it is **contractive**); a learned block carries no such guarantee. Some loops diverge, and Huginn's analysis (lesson 7) finds tokens whose states orbit or drift instead of settling.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: Why full fine-tuning is expensive, and why it may not need to be
md: Fine-tuning a pretrained model seems to move it along very few useful directions. LoRA turns that observation into an engineering bet: the *change* to each weight matrix during adaptation has low rank (the rank of a matrix is how many independent directions its outputs can point in), so it can be trained and stored as a small factorized update.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: A training recipe: learning rate, rank, alpha, dropout and evaluation
md: Recipe: sweep the learning rate up to the highest stable value (about 10x full fine-tuning's); scale alpha with rank (alpha = 2r, or rsLoRA); try a larger LR for B (LoRA+); use small dropout only for small data; budget activations, not just weights; never merge into a 4-bit base; and track a forgetting score next to the task score.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Unlearning by replacement: Who's Harry Potter and RMU
md: Replacement methods give the model something specific to do instead: predict generic tokens (WHP) or produce scrambled activations on hazardous inputs (RMU). That avoids gradient ascent's collapse, but the target behavior is defined only on the inputs you trained on.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: How a Mac defends itself: the layers from boot to app
md: Each macOS control answers one question. When you investigate a Mac incident, ask which question the attacker never had to face: was the code never quarantined, was it signed and notarized, did the user approve a prompt, did it run as a script rather than an app?

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: Endpoint Security: the API every Mac EDR is built on
md: Endpoint Security is to a Mac what kernel callbacks plus ETW (Event Tracing for Windows) are to Windows: the one place a security product can see every exec, file open, login and permission change, and block some of them. When choosing a Mac EDR, ask which ES events it subscribes to and which it uses in AUTH mode.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: The malware economy: loaders, access brokers and RaaS
md: Ransomware is the last step of a chain, not the first. Loader infections, sold remote-access logins and hands-on intrusion usually come days or weeks before encryption, which is your window to detect and evict.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Command and control: beacons, jitter and Cobalt Strike
md: Regular is not the same as malicious. Software updaters, mail clients, telemetry and monitoring agents all beacon. Use regularity to rank what to review, then check the destination (age of domain, reputation, who else talks to it) and the process that made the connections (Sysmon event 3).

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: Truncate, then re-normalize: the mechanics on a toy vector
md: Re-normalizing the query alone never changes a ranking: it scales every score by the same number. What changes rankings is the documents' prefix lengths, so re-normalize the stored document prefixes (or compute true cosine). OpenAI's embedding guide says the same: if you shorten vectors yourself, normalize them.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, CP, MoE, FP8 and MFU
lessonTitle: Tensor parallelism: column and row splits of the MLP and attention
md: Misconception: more TP is a free way to save memory. Per-GPU TP traffic stays near 8bsh per layer however large t gets, every GEMM gets t times smaller (lower GPU efficiency), and once t exceeds the GPUs in one server the all-reduces leave NVLink for the much slower network. Narayanan et al.'s Takeaway 1: use TP up to the server size (8 on DGX A100), then PP across servers.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, CP, MoE, FP8 and MFU
lessonTitle: FP8 training with Transformer Engine in Megatron Core
md: Mismatched recipes fail quietly. For a run that converges slower than its BF16 baseline, the low-precision guide's first check is that the recipe matches the hardware table, because a mismatched recipe silently falls back to slower paths.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Finding processes: walking the list versus scanning for tags
md: Scanning finds what the list misses, and also things that are no longer true: exited processes and stale copies of live ones. A psscan-only entry with an exit time is history; one without an exit time whose PID is not in the list is the interesting case.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Case: Ivanti Connect Secure, and a memory-first workflow
md: Memory is where code without files, decrypted configs, live connections and the attacker's last commands live, and it is the first evidence to disappear. Capture it early, verify it, and trust only what two independent views agree on.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: Why two threads can disagree about what happened first
md: Reordering is invisible to the thread that does it and visible to every other thread. Memory orderings are a portable contract about which reorderings other threads are allowed to observe.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Hazard pointers: announce exactly what you are reading
md: Hazard pointers: publish the address, fence, re-validate, then dereference. Retire into a private list and scan when it reaches R. Garbage is bounded by N x R even if threads stall.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: What memory safety means and why breaking it is dangerous
md: A common misconception: "if it didn't crash, it worked". An out-of-bounds write that lands in another variable usually does not crash at all. The program keeps running with corrupted data, which is often worse than crashing.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Why memory-safe languages remove whole bug classes
md: Memory-safe languages do not make programs bug-free, but they turn the bug classes of this course from silent corruption into compile errors or clean crashes. About two thirds of severe bugs in big C and C++ codebases are memory bugs, so moving new code to memory-safe languages removes most of the worst bugs at the source.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Measuring re-ID: rank-1, mAP, the Market-1501 protocol, re-ranking
md: Report mAP alongside rank-1, follow the cross-camera protocol, and compare methods only with the same tricks and the same re-ranking setting, because tricks alone can move rank-1 by about 7 points.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Miles in one picture: slime's loop built for frontier scale
md: Nearly every Miles feature in this course attacks one of two failure modes: GPUs waiting on each other (throughput), or the trainer computing gradients for something other than what was sampled (fidelity).

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Low-precision RL: formats, scales and the precision contract
md: "BF16 train, FP8 serve" is the lowest-friction mode, but it is not a contract: the docs say there is precision drift between the two paths, and on MoE workloads you should pair it with R3 and optionally TIS.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: Learned indexes: a model that predicts where a key lives
md: Model execution must be nearly free. The paper's first attempt ran a 2-layer, 32-neuron net through TensorFlow from Python: about 80,000 ns per prediction, versus about 300 ns for a whole B-tree traversal. Their Learning Index Framework instead extracts the trained weights and generates small C++ index code, never calling TensorFlow at lookup time.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Static analysis: decompile, read the manifest, search the code
md: Misconception: "the URL is in the app, so it's fine to leave the bucket open: only our app knows it." Anything in the package is public (lesson 2). A storage URL, an API key or a hidden endpoint in an app is a published address.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Running a mobile app assessment end to end, and where to practise
md: A mobile assessment is three tests in one: the package (what anyone can read), the platform (what other apps and the device can reach) and the backend (what the server actually enforces). Most serious findings sit in the last two.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: MLA in production: kernels, prefill, parallelism, FP8 cache
md: MLA moves the cost of attention from memory to compute: one 576-wide row per token per layer, read by every head. That is a big win for decode, where memory traffic dominates, as long as you keep many heads on the GPU that holds the cache and use the non-absorbed form when compute dominates.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Multi-LoRA across GPUs: tensor parallelism for adapters
md: Under tensor parallelism, split each adapter so its splits line up with the base: A along the rank (column layers) or rows (row layers), B along the output columns. Only rank-sized vectors cross GPUs, and the last result rides the base all-reduce.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: Union versus RRF, and deduplicating by document id
md: Union and RRF are not interchangeable. A union returns everything (N x k documents at worst) in retrieval order, so taking its first k usually just returns the first query's list. Pick RRF when the next stage has a fixed budget; pick union when a reranker will score all candidates anyway.

courseTitle: Multi-stage retrieval: designing the retrieve-then-rerank cascade
lessonTitle: LLM listwise reranking and distilling it into cheaper stages
md: **Distillation** turns an expensive stage into a teacher for a cheaper one. Run the slow model offline on training queries, then train a fast model to imitate its rankings. You pay the teacher's cost once, at training time, instead of on every query.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Shampoo: one preconditioner for the rows, one for the columns
md: A frequent mistake is to read $L^{-1/4}$ as an elementwise power. It is a *matrix* power: eigendecompose $L = Q \Lambda Q^\top$ and take $Q \Lambda^{-1/4} Q^\top$. That needs float32 (or better) and an eigensolver, which is why roots are only refreshed every $f$ steps.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Muon in a real training stack: parameter groups, sharding and code
md: Give Muon the hidden 2D matrices (Q, K, V kept separate), AdamW everything else. In PyTorch that is two optimizers stepped together. Distributed, Muon costs one extra bf16 gather per matrix and every rank's Newton-Schulz on the full matrix, against one fewer state buffer than AdamW.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: Why 'maximal': kernel, mean-field and feature-learning limits
md: Every stable parametrization is, at large width, either a kernel machine with frozen features or a feature learner. muP is the feature learner in which every layer moves as much as stability allows: that is what "maximal update" means.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: What muP does not transfer: horizon, weight decay, the SP debate
md: muP transfers across width; depth needs a branch rule; the token horizon needs an LR correction (about $D^{-0.32}$ at large scale); weight decay needs its $\eta\lambda$ timescale held fixed; regularization needs retuning.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: Locks in real systems: kernels, priorities and choices
md: Choosing a lock: in application code use the standard mutex, which is already uncontended-fast and spin-then-sleep. Reach for a pure spin lock only where the holder cannot be preempted and sections are tiny, as in a kernel with preemption disabled. Reduce contention itself (shorter sections, or sharding: splitting the data into parts that each have their own lock) before tuning spin counts.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Serializable Snapshot Isolation: catching dangerous structures
md: SSI has **false positives**. Not every dangerous structure is part of a real cycle, so some aborted transactions would have been fine. The paper reports serialization failure rates well under 1% on its benchmarks and an overall cost under 7% versus plain snapshot isolation, but your workload may differ.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: Few labels, new domain, and the failure modes that remain
md: When labels are scarce, spend them on **measurement** first and **training** second. A few hundred carefully labelled lines plus a pile of noisily labelled ones beats a thousand rushed labels with no held-out set, because without a trustworthy eval you cannot tell whether any change helped.

courseTitle: Nation-state cyber operations and cyber conflict
lessonTitle: Responses: naming, indictments, sanctions and disruption
md: Do not assume a response worked because it happened. Indicted officers keep working from home; sanctioned groups keep stealing; botnets are rebuilt from new unpatched devices. Measured effects are rarely public, and even the UK's NCF says measuring the effect of covert operations "is often very hard". Report what was done, and what is known about what changed.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: Three branches: compress, select, and slide
md: The gates are independent sigmoids, not a softmax. They do not have to sum to 1, so the model can turn several branches up or down at once. Also note what NSA does *not* do: it keeps the full KV cache (and three branches with independent keys and values), so it cuts the bytes *read* per step, not the bytes *stored*.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: Searching millions of hashes: BK-trees and multi-index hashing
md: MIH is fast only when substring buckets stay small. Norouzi et al. analyze uniformly distributed codes and find a substring length of about log2 of the database size works well. Highly skewed hashes (many near-blank images with the same hash) create giant buckets. PDQ's quality score, a 0 to 100 measure of how much detail an image has (next lesson), flags such featureless images so they can be filtered out.

courseTitle: NeMo RL: NVIDIA's Ray-based post-training library
lessonTitle: Running for real: metrics, checkpoints, export and a multi-node recipe
md: In all three published runs generation takes about half the step or more. Read your own `timing/train/` split before tuning: if generation dominates, the levers are vLLM parallelism and memory (lesson 4), non-colocated async generation (lesson 5) and response length, not the training backend.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: RST injection and the history of TCP session hijacking
md: Address-based trust is the real bug behind classic hijacking. Any system that grants access because a packet claims a source IP (old rsh, IP allow lists alone, zone transfers allowed by address) is relying on something an attacker can forge. Use cryptographic authentication.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: From overview to stream: the Wireshark workflow, decryption and tshark
md: A key log file is the key to every session it lists. Treat it like a password file: create it only for test traffic on your own machine, store it with the capture under the same protection, and delete both when done. Never set SSLKEYLOGFILE on a machine others use.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Extracting files from traffic: reassembly, true types and hashes
md: A hash lookup that returns nothing does not mean a file is safe: new and targeted malware is unknown by definition. Treat unknown executables from unusual sources as suspicious until analysed.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: Routing: gateways, TTL, traceroute and BGP
md: Routing is decided hop by hop from tables, and the most specific matching prefix wins. On the internet those tables are built from announcements other networks make, which BGP accepts on trust unless someone filters or validates them.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: First touch: the thread that writes a page first picks its node
md: Reading is not touching. The `mbind(2)` man page notes that a first *read* of an anonymous page maps a shared page of zeros held by the kernel; no page is allocated on your node until the first *write*. A warm-up loop that only reads does not place anything.

courseTitle: NVMe and SSD internals: FTL, garbage collection, write amplification
lessonTitle: Garbage collection and the write amplification formula
md: A drive does not know which LBAs your file system considers free. Unless told (lesson 4), every LBA ever written counts as live. Agrawal et al. put it bluntly: unlike a log-structured file system (one that, like an FTL, appends every write to a log and cleans it, but knows which files were deleted), the disk here is always full, so cleaning pressure is maximal all the time.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Scoring a detector: precision, recall, AP and COCO mAP
md: AP measures ranking quality across all thresholds for one class; COCO mAP averages it over 10 IoU thresholds and all classes. When comparing papers, check which one is reported: AP50 and AP@[.5:.95] differ a lot for the same model.

courseTitle: Object storage-backed databases: S3-native and tiered storage
lessonTitle: Tiered storage versus S3-native: choosing a design
md: Tiered storage moves *old* data to S3 and leaves the write path alone. S3-native moves the *write path itself* to S3, trading commit latency for stateless compute. Hybrids like Neon put a small quorum log in front so commits stay fast while object storage holds the bulk.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: SLOs, error budgets, burn-rate alerts, and the 03:00 dashboard
md: Alert on symptoms, not causes. The SRE book's advice is to focus much more effort on catching symptoms than causes, and to worry about a cause only when it is very definite and very imminent. A page saying "cache hit rate dropped" is a cause; a page saying "users are burning the checkout budget at 20x" is a symptom, and it stays correct when the cause next time is something else.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Adding layout: from LayoutLM boxes to OCR-free Donut
md: Layout-aware models add *where* to *what*: each word's box becomes embedding lookups, so a model can learn that a value sits right of its key. OCR-free models fold reading into the network and emit structure directly.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Linux capabilities: splitting root into pieces
md: `docker run --privileged` gives the container all capabilities and access to all host devices (Docker documentation). Treat it as running the workload as root on the host. The same goes for adding `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` or `CAP_SYS_MODULE` "just for one feature".

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Ethics and law first: public is not the same as permitted
md: Red lines in this course: no locating, profiling or tracking of specific private individuals; no misrepresentation to get access; no use of credentials or data from breaches; no publishing of personal details. Worked examples use your own organisation, a fictional company (Northwind, under the reserved `.example` domain) or public institutions and already-public cases.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Metadata: what photos and documents say about themselves
md: Files describe themselves. Read metadata as one clue that needs corroboration; remove it from everything you publish.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: People-search sites, data brokers and protecting your own footprint
md: Check only your own accounts, or colleagues' with their consent. Looking up someone else's email in breach data or a broker profile, without a lawful basis, is exactly the profiling this course rules out.

courseTitle: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
lessonTitle: Targets, PUBLIC vs PRIVATE, and why links fail
md: Declare every real dependency on the target that uses it, with the narrowest correct scope: PRIVATE if only the .cpp files use it, PUBLIC if your headers expose it, INTERFACE if only your headers do. CMake then derives include paths, definitions and link order for you.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: Diagnosing and fixing flaky tests: order, state and timing
md: Do not add `@pytest.mark.flaky` or `xfail` to a test your PR broke. Maintainers read that as hiding a failure. If you believe a failure is pre-existing flakiness, show evidence: the same test failing on `main` or on other PRs, or a seed that reproduces it without your change.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: Review by email: patch versions and trailer tags
md: You may not add a Reviewed-by, Tested-by or Acked-by tag for someone just because they said nice things. The kernel guide says these need the named person's explicit permission; only Cc:, Reported-by: and Suggested-by: can be added with implicit permission.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: AI-assisted contributions: label it, keep a human in the loop, or not
md: Before using an AI tool on a contribution, find the project's policy (CONTRIBUTING, developer docs, or the docs on patch submission). Then: never submit what you cannot explain, disclose as the project asks, and never let a tool add your sign-off.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Pushing rewritten history: --force-with-lease and its limits
md: `--force-with-lease` says "overwrite only if the remote is still what I last fetched". Add `--force-if-includes` so a fetch alone does not count as having seen the remote's commits.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: Inbound licensing: inbound=outbound and contributor agreements
md: The most common CLA failure is an email mismatch: the commits use a personal or unregistered address while the agreement (or the employer's group) lists another. Fix the author email and rewrite the commits, not the agreement.

courseTitle: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
lessonTitle: Is the difference real? t-tests, U tests and p-values
md: Significant is not the same as large. benchstat's docs stress that with enough low-noise data even very small changes become significant. Report the size of the change and its spread, and use the test only to answer "is this more than noise?"

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: What a maintainer needs: a failure they can run themselves
md: A bug report's first job is to let the maintainer make the failure happen themselves. Everything else in the report (description, guesses about the cause) comes second.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: Intermittent bugs, seeds, and environment differences
md: A flaky repro is not done until it fails every time or you know its failure rate. Pin seeds and inputs, report versions, and repeat runs enough times that a PASS means something.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: Self-review the diff, then use drafts to signal readiness
md: Self-review first, then mark ready. A reviewable PR is focused, explained, clean, and honestly labeled as draft or ready.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Automatic prefix caching in vLLM: hashing full blocks
md: A cache hit needs the whole prefix up to a block boundary to match. Chained hashes make that a sequence of dictionary lookups, and keeping freed blocks cached until they are actually reallocated makes eviction LRU for free.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Authorisation: scope, rules of engagement and permission
md: If something is not written in the scope, it is out of scope. When a new system appears mid-test (a subdomain, an extra address range), stop and get written approval to add it. PTES names scope creep as a common failure, especially during retesting.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Reporting: from finding to fix, and the retest
md: A finding is done when the client can understand it, verify it safely, fix the cause as well as the symptom, and see it marked closed after a retest.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: A profiling workflow, its costs and its blind spots
md: The workflow: record with a modest rate and working stacks, fold, filter, draw, read top edges, fix the widest plateau that you can change, then measure again.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: The persuasion levers every lure pulls
md: Misconception: "spotting bad grammar catches phishing". Spelling mistakes were never the core of a lure, and well-written messages are now easy to produce: the FBI's 2025 IC3 report notes businesses reported over USD 30 million in losses to BEC scams involving AI. Train on the levers and the process rules, not on typos.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Layered defences and the analyst workflow for a reported phish
md: The NCSC also warns that punishing people for clicking simulated phish erodes trust and stops them reporting real mistakes; it starts to resemble entrapment. Teach the levers and process rules (lesson 2), make reporting effortless, and celebrate reports.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: Rust layout: default repr, repr(C), and niches
md: C keeps your field order and you are responsible for packing it well. Rust's default repr may reorder fields and use niches to save space, but promises no exact layout. Use `#[repr(C)]` whenever bytes cross a boundary your compiler does not control.

courseTitle: Post-quantum cryptography and migration
lessonTitle: Five families, one competition and two spectacular breaks
md: What defenders take from 2022: young algorithms can fail completely, and to classical math. Hence three habits used throughout this course: **hybrids** during the transition (security holds if either component does), **diversity** (HQC as a backup on different math; SLH-DSA relying only on hashes) and **crypto agility**, so that replacing an algorithm is a configuration change rather than a rewrite.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Post-filtering: why top-k comes back short
md: Database textbooks sometimes say a filter is *highly selective* when it keeps very few rows, the opposite direction to the ratio. When reading docs, check whether they mean the ratio $s$ or the strictness. Here, small $s$ always means few matches.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Multi-tenancy: partition, shard or filter
md: Per-tenant graphs and shards make cross-tenant search expensive. If the product needs global queries (an admin search, analytics across customers), Qdrant documents that global requests without the tenant filter are slower, and Weaviate's multi-tenant collections require a tenant name on every query. Decide that requirement before choosing a layout.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: What privacy engineering protects, beyond keeping secrets
md: Privacy engineering reviews every data action, not only every attacker. NIST's objectives give the questions: will people be surprised (predictability), can we find and change or delete one person's data (manageability), and does the system know who is who more than it needs to (disassociability)?

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: When k-anonymity fails: l-diversity and t-closeness
md: l-diversity and t-closeness reduce attribute disclosure in one table under one attacker model. They do not compose across releases and they give no guarantee against unanticipated background knowledge.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Case: the 2020 US Census adopts differential privacy
md: A published epsilon is a starting point for review, not a verdict. Ask what the unit of privacy is, how the budget is split across tables and geographies, and what error users can tolerate. The Census case shows that both privacy and accuracy are political as well as technical choices.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Data protection impact assessments that change the design
md: A DPIA written after launch, or one whose risk section lists only security threats to the company, misses the point. It must be done before processing, assess necessity, and score harm to the individuals in the data.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Windows escalation 1: unquoted paths and weak service permissions
md: Run the path audit and the ACL audit together. An unquoted path with no writable folder before it is a hygiene fix; with one, it is a working escalation to SYSTEM.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Build it: train a small PRM and rerank with it
md: A PRM is a token classifier whose labels sit only on step separators; the rest of the sequence is ignored by the loss. Train and score with identical tokenization, then judge it two ways: does it pick better answers, and does it find the first wrong step.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: Linux: every thread is a task, and clone() picks what to share
md: Misconception: "threads are cheap because the kernel treats them as lighter objects." On Linux a thread and a process are the same kind of task. A thread is cheaper to create because there is less to set up (no new address space or page tables), and switching between two threads of one process is cheaper because the address space stays loaded. Those savings come from sharing, not from a different kind of object.

courseTitle: Product quantization (PQ)
lessonTitle: Why billion-vector indexes need compressed codes
md: PQ builds an exponentially large codebook, $(k^*)^m$ centroids, out of $m$ tiny ones. Each vector costs $m \log_2 k^*$ bits no matter how many dimensions it has.

courseTitle: Automatic prompt optimization: APE, OPRO and DSPy
lessonTitle: Managed prompt optimizers and a practical workflow
md: A rewrite produced without evaluation data is a hypothesis, not a result. Treat it like a candidate from a proposer: score it on your validation set against the current prompt before shipping.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Text versus bytes: what a computer actually stores
md: Text is characters, bytes are numbers. Decode at the edge of your program (when you read), work with `str` inside, and encode again only when you hash, send or write bytes.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Encodings: base64, hex and URL encoding, and why attackers use them
md: Encoding is reversible formatting, not secrecy. Normalize data (decode, lowercase, refang) before matching it, and expect attackers to stack encodings to slip past exact-match rules.

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: Expanding with models: doc2query, query2doc and HyDE
md: These numbers come from specific benchmarks (MS MARCO, TREC DL) and specific models. Measure on your own queries with judged results before adopting any expansion: a gain on average can still hurt many individual queries.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: RaBitQ indexing: normalize, rotate randomly, keep the signs
md: RaBitQ indexing: center and normalize, apply one random rotation, store the sign bits plus two floats per vector. The codebook is the rotated hypercube, so no k-means training is needed.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Workflows as state machines: skipping, repeating and reordering steps
md: Enforce workflows as explicit state machines on the server. For every request ask: is this action allowed from the state this object is in right now? If the only thing enforcing the order is the user interface, the order is not enforced.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Idempotency keys: safe retries, and what they do not stop
md: Look at line four of the output. Idempotency keys are chosen by the client, so an attacker racing a coupon or a withdrawal simply sends a different key with each request. Keys make honest retries safe; they do nothing for limits. The limit itself still needs lesson 9's atomic check.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Paxos: choosing one value with prepare and accept
md: A Paxos proposer is not free to pick its value. After phase 1 it must adopt the value of the highest-numbered proposal any acceptor in its majority reports. That single rule is what keeps a chosen value from ever changing.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: Prompting the generator to answer with citations
md: A citation is a claim, not a proof. The model can attach [3] to a sentence [3] does not support, as it did here. ALCE found even the best models lacked complete citation support about 50% of the time on ELI5 (Explain Like I'm Five: open-ended how and why questions from a Reddit forum), so check citations automatically rather than trusting their presence.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: Cutoff metrics and the divisors hidden inside them
md: Every cutoff metric hides a choice: the cutoff, the relevance threshold (grade at least 1 here), the divisor, and what to do with short runs. Two papers both reporting "MAP@10" may be computing different numbers.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: The way in: brokers, stolen logins and edge devices
md: MFA is necessary and not sufficient. Session theft (Citrix Bleed), help desk resets and unpatched appliances all walk past a password-plus-code login. Close each door with the control that fits it, and verify by testing, not by policy.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Why sockets cost microseconds and cores, and what RDMA removes
md: RDMA is not "the OS is gone". The kernel driver still creates queues, pins and maps memory, and handles errors. What disappears is per-message kernel work. That split between a slow **control path** and a fast **data path** is the design of the whole API.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: The authoritative server and its fixed tick
md: An authoritative server makes the server state the only truth. Every latency trick in the next lessons changes only what the *client displays*; none of them lets a client decide the outcome.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Implicit feedback: preference, confidence and weighted ALS
md: Do not drop the zeros. Training only on observed implicit events (all with p = 1) lets the model predict 1 everywhere and still reach zero loss. The low-confidence zeros are what make the scores discriminative.

courseTitle: Measuring size from a reference marker
lessonTitle: Why one pixels-per-mm ratio fails on a tilted photo
md: A common misconception is that the pixels-per-mm method only fails at extreme angles. In this toy, a moderate 40 degree tilt already puts it 15 percent off. Under perspective, scale varies with both position and direction across the plane.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: How the planner chooses: join order search and row estimates
md: The planner is only as good as its row estimates. It searches join orders exhaustively by dynamic programming up to a limit, then genetically; but a 100x row misestimate can turn the cheapest-looking plan into the slowest. Read EXPLAIN ANALYZE estimates against actuals first.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: A precise test: when is a proxy unhackable?
md: Unhackability is a very strong condition. For rich policy classes, every proxy that is not simply equivalent to the true reward (same ranking of all policies) can be hacked by some policy. Skalse et al. conclude that learned rewards are better treated as aids to policy learning than as specifications to optimize without limit. The practical question becomes how far you can optimize before hacking appears.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: From gaming to tampering: reward tampering and in-context hacking
md: Misconception: reward hacking only happens during RL training. ICRH needs no gradient at all. An agent with frozen weights, a goal and a feedback loop optimizes in context, and its side effects grow with each cycle.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Monte Carlo: simulating 100,000 years of losses
md: Simulate, do not multiply point estimates. The mean of the simulation is the ALE; the percentiles describe bad years; and a typical year (the median) may cost nothing at all, which is exactly why risk without numbers is easy to ignore until it happens.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: SOC 2: trust services criteria, Type I vs II, and your evidence
md: Read the **exceptions** and the **complementary user entity controls** (CUECs) sections of any vendor's SOC 2. Exceptions are where the auditor found a control did not operate. CUECs are controls the vendor assumes *you* perform (for example, "customers are responsible for enabling MFA for their users"); if you do not, the vendor's report does not cover that risk.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Third-party risk: questionnaires, SBOMs and concentration risk
md: A questionnaire is a vendor's own claims. "Yes" to every question from a 20-person startup is a signal to ask for evidence, not a pass. And a vendor that is excellent at security can still be a concentration risk: CrowdStrike was the security control, not the attacker. Score both "how likely is this vendor to be breached" and "what happens to us if this vendor stops working for a day".

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: One RL step is five workloads on two kinds of engine
md: A common misconception is that a bigger training cluster speeds up RL roughly linearly. Training is often a minority of the step. If generation is two-thirds of the time, even infinitely fast training saves at most a third.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Training-inference mismatch: same weights, different logprobs
md: "Same checkpoint" does not mean on-policy. Two engines with identical weights are two different policies at the level of logprobs, and the gap grows with FP8 rollout, MoE routing and long sequences. Treat the rollout engine as a behavior policy and log the gap every step.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: One fault, 397 alerts: collapsing the storm
md: Dedup and grouping are lossless: they change how many notifications you receive, not what was observed. Inhibition and silences are lossy: they delete evidence from your view. Use the first two freely and the last two sparingly.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: How k shapes the curve 1/(k + r)
md: Do not confuse RRF's k with the k of k-nearest-neighbors. Azure AI Search's docs stress that the RRF constant is "entirely separate" from the k that sets how many neighbors a vector query returns. Elasticsearch names them `rank_constant` and `rank_window_size` to avoid the clash.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Bindings, helpers, abstractions: the layers under a Rust driver
md: Misconception: "Rust drivers do not need cleanup code." They need exactly as much cleanup as C drivers. The difference is that it lives once in a `Drop` impl (yours or an abstraction's) and runs on every path automatically, including early returns from `?`.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: What Rust in the kernel does not prevent, and what it costs
md: Rust in the kernel moves a large class of bugs (forgotten unlocks, unchecked errors, use-after-free through ownership mistakes) from runtime to compile time, and concentrates the rest into small, documented `unsafe` regions. It does not remove the need for review, lockdep, or testing.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Worked example: weighted vtime fairness in a few lines of BPF
md: scx_simple charges `SCX_SLICE_DFL - p->scx.slice`. Its own comment warns that a task that yields has its slice zeroed and so is charged a full slice. Precise schedulers take explicit timestamps in `running` and `stopping` instead.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Safety net, failure modes and schedulers in production
md: Misconception: switching to a sched_ext scheduler is a free speedup. Each one encodes tradeoffs for a workload. scx_simple's own header says it suits a single uniform L3 and that its FIFO mode lets saturating threads drown out interactive ones. Benchmark your workload against the fair class (lesson 10 shows how), and check whether the scheduler honors the cgroup limits you rely on.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Key ceremonies: the DNS root key and multi-person control
md: Multi-person control turns "trust this administrator" into "trust that M of these N people did not all collude", and a recorded ceremony turns it into something auditors and outsiders can verify.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Python: eval, pickle and yaml.load turn data into code
md: Ask of every parser in a diff: can this input make the parser call code? If yes (eval, pickle, unsafe YAML), the input must never come from outside the trust boundary. Pick a format that can only describe data.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Go: ignored errors, text/template and Go's review tools
md: Go review checklist: every `_` in an error position (what zero value flows on?), every shared map and variable (which lock?), every map field (who calls make?), html/template for HTML and every template.HTML conversion, and gosec, go vet, govulncheck and go test -race in CI.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Writing the finding and the fix so it gets merged
md: Do not overstate. "Critical, full compromise" on a bug that needs admin access and a rare configuration teaches developers to ignore your severities. Do not understate either: "minor input handling issue" for code execution gets it scheduled next quarter. State exactly what you proved and what you believe but did not prove.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: RADIUS and TACACS+: central logins for network devices
md: RADIUS and TACACS+ secrets are often short, reused across hundreds of devices, and left in device configuration backups. Anyone holding the secret and a packet capture can recover RADIUS passwords and forge replies. Treat the secret like a password database key: long, random, unique per device or site, and rotated.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Brewer-Nash's Chinese Wall, and choosing the right model
md: A formal model is a precise statement of what secure means for one kind of system. Pick the model by the harm you fear: disclosure, contamination, invalid change, or conflict of interest. Real systems combine several.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Segmentation and microsegmentation, planned from real traffic
md: Segmenting by host pairs is not the finish line. The billing app still talks to the domain controller; restrict that flow to the authentication ports it needs and to the app's own identity, and watch it closely.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: LLMs from zero: tokens, sampling and confident mistakes
md: Treat an LLM like a fast, fluent junior analyst who has never seen your environment, gives slightly different answers each time, sometimes invents facts, and believes whatever text it is shown.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Threat, vulnerability, exploit, payload and risk
md: A vulnerability is not a risk by itself. A severe bug in software you do not run, or on a machine with no network connection, may carry very little risk. A boring weakness on an internet-facing system that attackers already scan for can carry a lot. Lesson 6 turns this into a patching order.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: EternalBlue and WannaCry: a patch, a leak and a worm
md: WannaCry: one wormable bug, a patch two months old, a leaked exploit, and organisations that had not patched or could not patch old systems. The fixes were basic: patch, remove legacy protocols, filter port 445, segment, back up.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: What a security leader is for: the CISO's job and reporting line
md: Misconception: "a higher reporting line means better security". The reporting line decides two things: whether bad news can be filtered before it reaches the people who decide, and whether the CISO is grading their own boss's work. A CISO under the CEO with no budget and no board access can be weaker than one under a CIO with a standing audit-committee slot.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: Vendors and tools: buy, build, consolidate and plan the exit
md: A capability label is not a capability. "Log search" in a SIEM with a year of retention and in an XDR add-on with 30 days are different things for an investigation that looks back three months (recall dwell time in *Preparation*). Before retiring a tool: compare depth and retention, count integrations and detections built on it, check the contract's end date, and run both in parallel for a period.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: Regulators and disclosure: materiality, risk factors, certifications
md: Writing "a breach could harm us" in a filing after a breach has happened is not cautious; the SEC treated it as a misleading half-truth. When a risk has materialised, say so in proportion. And never let a public statement (filing, trust page, customer questionnaire) say more than your internal records support.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Incident updates when you do not know yet
md: Never let an update outrun the evidence to sound reassuring. A confident claim that later proves wrong costs more trust than an honest "not yet known". The next lesson is a real case.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Inside the search tree: selection, expansion, evaluation and backup
md: A common bug: backing up $v$ with the same sign at every level. Then the edge into a leaf is credited with the value for the player who did not choose it, and each player's search prefers moves that are good for the opponent. Store each $Q$ from the point of view of the player who made the move, and flip the sign once per ply.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Adversarial self-play for language models, and AlphaProof
md: Adversarial self-play gives an automatic curriculum, an opponent or proposer that keeps the task at the edge of ability. It does not by itself create a correct signal. The strongest results, from AlphaZero to AlphaProof, pair self-play with a judge that is never wrong.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: The server as a confused deputy
md: The server is trusted by its network, its cloud account and its own disk. Any feature that lets input choose *what the server touches* (a host, a path, a class, a lookup) lends that trust to the attacker. Defence means taking the choice away, or shrinking what the server can touch.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Path traversal and safe path joins
md: Common broken fixes: deleting `../` from the input once (nested sequences reassemble after the deletion), checking before URL-decoding (encoded dots slip through), checking the string starts with the base (`/srv/app/files-old` passes), and forgetting that on Windows the backslash `..\` works too. Normalise first, then compare whole path components.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Inside the server: three processes and an overlapped loop
md: Chunked prefill trades the long prompt's time to first token for bounded step size: lower peak activation memory (activations are the intermediate tensors a forward pass keeps, and they grow with the number of tokens in the pass) and, when decodes are mixed in, steadier token gaps for everyone else. It does not reduce total prefill work.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Bidirectional search and contraction hierarchies
md: CH trades a one-time preprocessing pass (contract nodes, add shortcuts) for tiny queries: two upward searches that meet at the most important node of the route, then shortcuts are unpacked back into original roads.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: One instruction, many lanes: SIMD registers and lane counts
md: Misconception: "wider vectors always mean proportionally faster code." Width is only the upper bound. Memory bandwidth, latency chains and loop overheads decide how much of it you actually get.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: Why a general-purpose heap wastes memory
md: Allocators are not just faster or slower `malloc`s. Each design gives up a freedom (free in any order, any size, any type) and gets speed or lower fragmentation in return. Ask which freedom your workload can give up.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Placing training and rollout: colocated or separate GPUs
md: "Disaggregated" here is about trainer versus rollout GPUs. It is unrelated to PD (prefill-decode) disaggregation (`--prefill-num-servers`), which puts SGLang's prefill (processing the whole prompt in one pass) and decode (generating one token at a time) on different servers, and it does not imply async training by itself.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Fully async rollout and the price of staleness
md: Async in slime means: same train.py, different rollout function, separate GPU pools. You trade a bounded amount of policy staleness for not waiting on the slowest trajectory.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: Ethereum accounts, transactions and gas
md: Gas is also a security limit. Each block has a gas cap, so a function whose work grows with user-controlled data (a loop over every depositor) can become impossible to call. The Solidity docs warn this "can cause the complete contract to be stalled". Lesson 9 shows the fix.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: Upgradeable proxies and storage collisions
md: In a proxy system, storage layout is part of the interface. Any write to the slot that holds the implementation address is an upgrade, whoever makes it. Detect: watch that slot's value every block, not just `Upgraded` events (Bybit's slot-0 overwrite emitted none), and run OpenZeppelin's upgrade-safety checks before each upgrade. Respond: a timelock leaves time to cancel a bad upgrade or let users exit.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: When the attacker calls the help desk: MFA resets and new devices
md: The help desk is part of your attack surface and part of your sensor network. Alert on MFA resets and new device enrollments for privileged users, correlate them with what happens next, and verify with the real person through a channel the caller cannot control. Okta also recommends stronger help desk identity checks, such as visual verification.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Security is a secondary task: why people work around it
md: Misconception: "people ignore security because they do not care". Adams and Sasse found people inventing their own schemes to comply, and Herley shows that ignoring costly advice is often the rational choice. When most people bypass a control, treat it as a design defect in the control.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Physical security in layers: zones, CPTED and access rules
md: Misconception: "physical security is the facilities team's job". Many intrusion paths end at a network port or an unlocked laptop. Security engineers should own the requirements (which zones protect which systems, what gets logged, how alerts reach the SOC) together with facilities.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Enforcing sparsity: L1, TopK and JumpReLU
md: L1 penalises size, so it shrinks every active latent. TopK (fixed k), Gated (separate gate) and JumpReLU (learned per-latent thresholds with an L0 penalty) all separate deciding which latents fire from estimating how big they are.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Where SAEs fall short: absorption, missing features and weak baselines
md: Sparsity rewards absorbing a parent feature into its children, so SAE latents can have silent holes. Matryoshka and BatchTopK reduce the damage, but SAEs are not canonical units, and on labelled tasks simple baselines such as difference-in-means and linear probes usually match or beat them.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Ordinary kriging: solving for the best weights
md: Kriging weights come from solving a linear system, not from a fixed formula. That lets them account for redundancy between sensors (declustering) and for sensors hidden behind others (screening), and it yields an error variance for every estimate.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: How many tokens per round, and what speedup to expect
md: Speedup is not tokens per pass. A draft that is accurate but slow (high alpha, high c) can lose to a weaker but nearly free one. Leviathan et al. found drafts about two orders of magnitude smaller than the target usually balanced alpha and c best.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: Whisper: a transformer over 30-second spectrogram windows
md: Whisper is an audio-conditioned language model. The encoder turns 30 s of log-mel into 1500 vectors; the decoder generates the transcript token by token, with language, task and timestamps expressed as tokens in the same sequence.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: The stack: memory that frees itself when a function returns
md: Stack memory lives exactly as long as the function call that created it. Allocation and release are a pointer adjustment, which is why the size must be bounded and why anything that must outlive the call has to go somewhere else: the heap.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: TLB reach, huge pages and shootdowns
md: TLB reach = entries x page size. Working sets beyond it pay a page walk on most random accesses; huge pages raise reach by 512 times, and every unmap in a multithreaded process may interrupt other CPUs.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Lab: build, sweep and evaluate a steering vector on a small chat model
md: Three things bite first attempts. The chat template inserts a default system prompt ("You are Qwen...") when you give none. Qwen's tokenizer turns "(A" into a single token, so the answer letter is not a separate position: read activations at the "(A" token and score the "(A" and "(B" tokens. And the hook must cope with both output types of a decoder layer. Print the tokens of one full prompt before anything else.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Windows, watermarks and allowed lateness, step by step
md: Watermark = the processor's estimate of how far event time has progressed. It decides when a window first fires; allowed lateness decides how long the window can still be corrected; anything beyond is dropped or side-output. Every choice trades latency for completeness.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Causal masks, teacher forcing and cross-attention
md: A causal mask sets the scores of future positions to minus infinity before softmax, so with teacher forcing every target position trains in one pass without seeing its own answer. Cross-attention is the same function with queries from the decoder and keys and values from the encoder.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Training recipe, quadratic cost and what changed since 2017
md: "Transformer" does not mean "GPT" (generative pre-trained transformer, OpenAI's line of decoder-only language models). The 2017 model is an encoder-decoder for translation. Decoder-only language models keep only its masked self-attention stack; encoder-only models keep only the unmasked encoder.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: Tuning k1 and b on a real test collection
md: Never tune on the queries you report. Use a dev split or cross-validation, and treat a flat surface as a sign that the defaults are fine: a 0.002 dev gain over the default is within noise for a few hundred queries.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Stacking blocks: residuals, pre-LayerNorm, MLP and a tied output head
md: A GPT is just: embed (token + position), $L$ x [pre-LN causal attention, pre-LN MLP, each added to the residual stream], final LayerNorm, project back to vocabulary scores with the tied embedding matrix.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Derivative rules and the chain rule for nested functions
md: A common slip is evaluating the outer derivative at $x$ instead of at the inner value. Here $f'(u) = 2u$ must use $u = 7$, giving 14, not $2 \times 2 = 4$. That is why the forward values are computed and stored first: the backward step needs them.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Gradient descent: walking downhill and choosing the step size
md: A rising loss does not always mean a bug in your gradients. With a correct gradient, too large a learning rate alone makes training diverge, as $\eta = 0.35$ did here. Lowering $\eta$ is the first thing to try.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Expansion and quoting: why rm $f can delete the wrong files
md: Do not test your quoting in zsh and assume bash agrees. zsh, the default interactive shell on macOS, does **not** word-split unquoted parameter expansions unless the `SH_WORD_SPLIT` option is set. Scripts that start with `#!/bin/bash` or `#!/bin/sh` (a first line naming the interpreter, the shebang of lesson 4) follow the splitting rules shown here.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Exit statuses and scripts that fail loudly
md: `set -e` is a safety net, not error handling. It misses failures inside functions called from conditions and in `&&` chains. For steps that matter, check explicitly: `if ! cp src dst; then echo 'copy failed' >&2; exit 1; fi`.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Learning word vectors by predicting their neighbours
md: Skip-gram is not trained to be a good language model; the prediction task is a pretext. Mikolov et al. say plainly that the skip-gram model is only concerned with learning high-quality vector representations. After training, the output layer is usually thrown away and the input vectors are kept as the embeddings.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Inside a GPU: many small cores fed by one big memory
md: A GPU is a throughput machine. It hides slow memory by keeping many warps in flight, not by making any single access fast. Give it too little parallel work and the SMs sit idle.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: The KV cache: why memory grows with every token
md: KV cache size = 2 x layers x KV heads x head dim x bytes, per token, per sequence. It grows linearly with context and with batch size, and it is usually what limits how many users one GPU can serve.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: From hello.c to a running process
md: Misconception: "the compiler makes something the CPU runs straight off the disk." The CPU only fetches instructions from memory. An executable is inert until the OS loader maps it into a process's memory and points the CPU at its entry point.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Where a program's memory lives: code, heap and stack
md: Never return a pointer to a local variable. Its stack slot is reused by the very next call (as the second call to square reused the first one's slot), so the pointer soon points at unrelated data. Use the heap (malloc) for data that must outlive the function.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Pretraining: next-token loss over trillions of tokens
md: A low pretraining loss does not mean a helpful model. The loss rewards matching the *distribution* of internet text, including its errors, rudeness and rambling. That is exactly why the later stages exist.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Where preference data comes from: guidelines, safety, AI feedback
md: Preference data is a design choice: who labels, under which guidelines, on which prompts, with which ratings. Separate signals (helpfulness and safety) and AI labels from written principles (RLAIF) are now standard ingredients of post-training.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Answering AND queries by merging postings
md: Skip pointers only help AND-style intersections, where we look for a specific docID. For OR we must output every posting of both lists anyway, so there is nothing to skip. Skips are also costly to maintain when postings lists change often.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Getting the top k fast: tiers, MaxScore and WAND
md: Safe top-k pruning keeps a running threshold, the k-th best score so far, and a score upper bound per term (or per block). Any document whose bounds cannot beat the threshold is skipped with the skip data, so the top k is exactly what exhaustive scoring would return.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Multi-file C: headers, include guards, static, extern and make
md: Headers hold declarations (`extern` variables, prototypes) behind an include guard; exactly one .c file holds each definition; `static` keeps helpers private. A Makefile lists what each file depends on, and make rebuilds only what is older than its inputs.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Object lifetimes: automatic, static and malloc'd memory
md: Before you keep a pointer, ask how long the object behind it lives. Locals die when their function returns, malloc'd memory dies at free, and realloc can retire the old address at any call.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Undefined behavior, and the tools that catch it
md: Develop C with `-Wall -Wextra -g -fsanitize=address,undefined` on, and fix every warning. Most of the pointer and lifetime bugs from this course then fail loudly at the exact line instead of corrupting memory silently.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Borrowing: many readers or one writer
md: Shared XOR mutable: any number of `&T`, or exactly one `&mut T`, never both at the same point in the program. A borrow is live from creation to last use.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: When the checker says no: clone, Rc and RefCell
md: Default to borrowing; move when the callee should keep the value; clone when copies are cheap or necessary; use `Rc`/`RefCell` only for data with genuinely shared ownership.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: A matrix is a function that moves every vector
md: $A\mathbf{x}$ is both a stack of dot products (one per row) and a weighted sum of columns. The columns of $A$ are the images of the basis vectors, so they fully describe the map.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Tensors, batches and broadcasting: shapes in real code
md: Broadcasting checks sizes, never meaning. A loss computed from (3, 1) predictions and (3,) targets averages 9 differences instead of 3 and raises nothing. Assert shapes where arrays from different places meet: `assert pred.shape == y.shape`.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Many features: linear regression in matrix form and feature scaling
md: With many features, predictions are $\hat y = Xw$ and the MSE gradient is $\frac{2}{n}X^\top(Xw - y)$. Its minimum solves the normal equations $X^\top Xw = X^\top y$. Features on very different scales stretch the bowl, so gradient descent crawls; standardizing them rounds it out.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Validation and penalties: choosing lambda, L2 and L1
md: Choose capacity and penalty strength by **validation** error and keep the test set for one final check. L2 (weight decay) shrinks every weight a little each step; L1 pins weak weights at exactly zero and so selects features.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Why a single linear layer cannot learn XOR
md: Misconception: a deeper network of linear layers is more expressive. It is not; it is exactly as expressive as one linear layer. Another one: universal approximation means any network will learn any function. It only guarantees that suitable weights exist.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Gradients through depth: vanishing, exploding and unlucky seeds
md: Backprop computes the exact gradient of the loss at the current weights; it does not guarantee a good solution. The loss surface of a network is not **convex** (bowl-shaped, so that every valley is the lowest one), so the starting point matters. Lesson: always check the loss curve, and try more than one seed.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Beyond physical memory: page faults, swapping and replacement
md: Memory is a cache for pages, and a disk-backed miss costs about 100,000 memory accesses. A replacement policy tries to approximate OPT using the past: LRU in principle, the use bit and the clock algorithm in practice, preferring clean pages.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Persistence: how a hard disk spends its time
md: A random disk I/O is almost all positioning: seek plus half a rotation, milliseconds, against microseconds of transfer. Make requests large and sequential, and let the scheduler order them by position.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Probability by counting outcomes, and what conditioning does
md: Conditioning means restricting attention to the outcomes consistent with what you know, then renormalizing so they sum to 1. Almost every formula in this course is that one idea applied carefully.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Covariance, correlation and the multivariate Gaussian
md: Correlation is not causation. Ice cream sales and sunburns are correlated because sunny weather drives both: a **confounder**, a third variable that causes both. The Deep Learning textbook by Goodfellow, Bengio and Courville makes the same point about conditioning: P(from Germany | speaks German) is high, but teaching someone German does not change where they are from.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Power and sample size: planning an A/B test before running it
md: Power depends on the effect size you assume. Choose the smallest effect worth acting on before you see data, not the effect you hope for and not the effect a finished test happened to show.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Run your own scaling study: sweep, fit, extrapolate, error bars
md: A scaling study is an experiment design problem: budgets spread over orders of magnitude, sizes that bracket each valley, a properly ended schedule per run, then two fits (IsoFLOP parabolas and the parametric form) that should agree, each with bootstrap error bars.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Average precision, MAP and MRR: one number for a whole ranking
md: A common bug: dividing by the number of relevant documents *retrieved* (4) instead of all relevant documents (5). That gives 0.642 instead of 0.513 and silently rewards systems that retrieve fewer relevant documents.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Online evaluation: clicks, position bias, A/B tests and interleaving
md: Interleaving says which system users prefer on a result page, and it needs clicks to work. It cannot measure effects beyond one page, such as revenue or whether users come back next week; those still need an A/B test.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Where dense retrieval fails: hybrid search and re-ranking
md: Each stage covers another's blind spot: BM25 for rare exact terms, the bi-encoder for meaning across different words, the cross-encoder for precise final ordering on a short list. Evaluate the whole pipeline on your own queries with the lab's metrics: recall@k for each first stage at the depth the re-ranker reads, nDCG@10 for the final list.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Build a byte-level BPE tokenizer in Python
md: Decode with `errors="replace"` (or keep bytes) whenever ids can be cut at arbitrary points: one token at a time while streaming, or a sequence the model generated that may not be valid UTF-8. With strict decoding a partial character raises an error. When streaming, keep the bytes and only show the characters once all their bytes have arrived.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Residual connections: why 56 layers trained worse than 20
md: A residual block computes $x + F(x)$. The identity path makes doing nothing easy to learn and gives the gradient a direct route to every layer. Start each branch near zero so that a deep stack begins as one identity map rather than a variance amplifier.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: HNSW, IVF, PQ and production indexes
lessonTitle: Why exact nearest-neighbor search stops scaling
md: ANN indexes trade a little recall for orders of magnitude fewer distance computations. Every ANN number you read (or report) should come as a pair: recall@k and speed, measured against exact brute-force results on the same queries.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: HNSW, IVF, PQ and production indexes
lessonTitle: Tuning ef and M, and choosing an index
md: Tune HNSW in this order: pick M for your data (12 to 48 is typical), set ef_construction high enough that build-time recall is near 1, then sweep ef at query time against brute-force ground truth until recall@k meets your target at acceptable latency.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Reproducible builds: proving a binary came from its source
md: Reproducible builds prove the binary matches *the source you built from*. They say nothing about which source that should be. xz 5.6.1's release tarball contained a malicious build script missing from git; rebuilding the tarball reproduces the backdoor perfectly. Compare release archives against the tagged git tree too (Arch Linux switched xz to building from git when the backdoor was disclosed).

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Reproduce collapse yourself: simulate the loops, measure diversity
md: A closed loop collapses at a rate set by the sample size, and you can measure that rate. A small but steady stream of real data turns the downward drift into a stable level.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: What a system call costs, and how to make fewer of them
md: Treat 150 cycles as a floor from 2010 hardware, not a current number. Since then kernels added mitigations on every entry and exit for CPU vulnerabilities: you can see `SWITCH_TO_KERNEL_CR3` (separate kernel page tables) and `IBRS_ENTER` (IBRS, Indirect Branch Restricted Speculation, limits branch speculation) in today's `entry_SYSCALL_64`. Measure on your own machine before quoting a number.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: Editing the map: munmap, mprotect, mremap and how exec builds it
md: The kernel's view of your memory is a list of VMAs. `execve` and ld.so create the first ones, `mmap` adds, `munmap` removes and splits, `mprotect` splits by permission, and `mremap` resizes or moves. `/proc/PID/maps` is that list, and it is the first thing to read when a mapping misbehaves.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Fan-out: why one server's p99 becomes everyone's problem
md: With fan-out N, the user-visible tail is set by roughly the 1 - 1/(100N) quantile of each component, not by its p99. A quantile is a percentile written as a fraction: the 0.99 quantile is p99. The formula is the N p at most 0.01 rule from the prediction, solved for p: each leaf may be slow at most 1/(100N) of the time. The wider the fan-out, the deeper into the tail you must measure and engineer.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: Diameter in 4G roaming: the same trust model on IP
